analytic.title: An Optimal Algorithm for Guaranteeing Sporadic Tasks in Hard Real-Time Systems

div.head: Guaranteeing that time critical tasks will meet their timing constraints is an important aspect of real-time systems research. Indeed, a real time system is dynamic and consequently requires on -line and adaptive scheduling strategies.
div.p: In this paper, we survey and extend results on scheduling hard deadline periodic and sporadic tasks on the monoprocessor model. The periodic tash are independent, run cyclically and their characteristics are known in advance.

div.head: In addition, we allow for the unpredictable arrival of aperiodic tasks said to be sporadic with hard real-time constraints. The problem is to jointly schedule the periodic and sporadic tasks so that the timing requirements for both sets of tasks are met.
div.p: This paper presents a schedulability test that permits to decide whether a new occurring task can be accepted. This test is built upon the Earliest Deadline scheduling algorithm which features a high performance and ease of implementation.

div.head: I-JNTRODUCTION
div.p: Progress in data transmission techniques and the decreasing cost of processors have made it possible to design processing systems whose decentralized and extensible structure is perfectly adapted to real time applications [Stankovic 881. Indeed, it has been recognized that it is natural to distribute control among several connected processors, allowing programs to be implemented as relatively indepedent tasks which run asynchronously exept for occasional synchronisation and communication. For many of these applications such as avionics, on line process control, etc ..., the programs called tasks must satisfy certain timing constraints determined by the physical process being controlled to avoid possible catastrophic results. In all these areas said to be hard real time, the most important quality the computer system should possess is reliability.
That is, it must respond to stimuli either external or internal within specific bounded intervals, else all the system fails.

This work was supported in part by C3 (CNRS) under EXORAT project TH0328-5/90/0000/0578/$01 .OO 0 1990 IEEE In this paper, we consider a distributed real-time system which consists of a set of monoprocessor nodes. Each node supports a set of periodic tasks assigned to it for all their lifetime and handled by a scheduling strategy to comply with all timing requirements. The periodic tasks typically arise from sensor data or control loops. The value of their period depends on the dynamic of the physical process that they control. Their distribution in the computer system is made initially by taking into account technological specifications such as dismbution of input and output ports.

An application may also implement non iterative tasks which generally arise from operator actions or asynchronous external events such as alarms. Their activation occurs at an unpredictable time and so, we suppose that at any instant, such a time critical task said to be sporadic may occur on a node and require to be run within a specified bounded time interval. This means that each node in the system has to cope dynamically with an unpredictable increase in processor workload that can affect the scheduling of periodic tasks and sporadic tasks already accepted on the node.
In such a system, the two problems to be solved on line are the followings:

1-Given the timing characteristics of the occumng task as well as the load inflected to the node of already assigned periodic and sporadic tasks, is it possible to insure a feasible execution for this task? 2-If the answer is negative, are there one or several nodes in the distributed system able to receive and feasibly execute this task without injuring the tasks already assigned? And how is one able to decide which node is the most suited to receive this task?

This last problem has been treated in [Ramamritham 841. There. a solution was proposed based on biddinE strategy. The node on which the sporadic task occurs broadcasts to all other nodes a request for bid message containing the timing characteristics of the task. The best bidder is then determined by evaluating for each node, its surplus processing power. For more details, see [Ramamritham 841 and [Zhao 851.

In this paper, we are particularly concemed with the first problem which consists of deciding whether a task that is newly O C C U K ~ on a node can be accepted by this node. This task may amve at a node either directly or as a request of a bidding process.

The question of the acceptance of a new task amounts to the question of the existence of a valid schedule i.e a schedule in which all the tasks will execute by their deadline. The answer then depends on timing parameters of all the tasks running on the machine such as execution times and deadlines. Besides these parameters, the scheduling strategy i.e the strategy of the assigning the processor to the tasks and the amount of the system overhead also affect the possibility of deadline missing and consequently the possibility of rejecting the new occurring task.

In what follows, we will present an acceptance algorithm which is both efficient in term of computational complexity and optimal in term of performance evaluation. By optimality, we mean that any sporadic task which is rejected by the test will be rejected by any other test. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section I1 is a background about dynamic scheduling of sporadic tasks. Section I n presents the theoretical foundation of our appraoch. Description of the acceptance algorithm is made in section IV. The paper concludes with a summary in section V.

In [Ramamritham 841, an acceptance test was developped with task independence assumed and then extended to consider precedence constraints [Cheng 861. Periodic and sporaric tasks are executed according to the Non Preemptive Earliest Deadline algorithm. To take into account overheads involved by implementation of the dispatcher, its run time is included in the computation time of each task. The acceptance test which has been proposed consists in constructing the schedule in which tasks are scheduled nonpreemptively as late as possible and then in verifying for each of them that the resulting latest start time is no earlier than the ready time. Overheads induced by this test are considered by executing the acceptance routine as a periodic task. Value of the period is determined by estimating the mean arrival rate for the sporadic tasks. However, as a sporadic task must be examined as soon as possible, an other alternative amounts to interrupt the running task immediately after the arrival of the sporadic task but after ascertaining that this could not cause the running task to miss its deadline.

Performance evaluation of this acceptance test was performed by a simulation program which results are given in [Ramamritham 841. The statistics include task response times and percentage of sporadic tasks that meet their deadline. However, results obtained by simulations are not sufficient to definitively conclude about the overall performance of this approach. It is natural to believe that they were useful1 if only to pick up indications about the behaviour of the heuristic approach followed to design the acceptance test. In summary, the main feature of the scheduling scheme proposed by Ramamritham and all lies in the two following points:
-all the overheads involved in scheduling are taken into consideration.
-the acceptance test is built around an heuristic since tasks are scheduled nonpreemptively.

Non preemptive scheduling is certainIy more practical than preemptive scheduling because of its simplicity and fewer overhead involved by its implementation. However, even in the monoprocessor case, optimal nonpreemptive scheduling is a I Whard problem and thus computationally intractable [Garey 791. It follows that construction of a schedule must be performed by heuristics. The nonpreemptive Earliest Deadline algorithm is the more realistic and adapted to real-time context but obviously will lead to lower processor utilization and so to reject more sporadic tasks than preemptive scheduling. A performance study by Woodside and Graig [Woodside 871 compared various nonpreemptive scheduling algorithms applied to a hard real-time system.

The preemptive Earliest Deadline (ED) scheduling algorithm is the optimum scheduling algorithm for deadline tasks [Serlin 721 [Liu 731 [Blazevicz 771. That is, any task set which cannot be feasibly scheduled by ED will not be feasibly scheduled by any other preemptive or non preemptive algorithm. In [Chetto 871, a first approach was proposed to solve the acceptance problem assuming that tasks are scheduled preemptively according to the ED algorithm. The test is achieved by considering the schedule for the periodic task set as a time rigid one and by recovering the idle time intervals in the schedule to process sporadic tasks. Clearly, this method lies in the ability to provide accurate indications about processor activity within any time interval. The algorithm that implements the test is efficient since it runs in polynomial time but only provides a sufficient acceptance condition. Although all the tasks, periodic and sporadic are effectively scheduled by ED algorithm, the test is made by treating the sporadic tasks as background tasks.

An optimal solution to the acceptance problem was given in [Chetto 89al under some restrictive hypothesis. In particular, it is assumed that, when any sporadic task arrives on a node and requires to be run, there is no other sporadic task, previously accepted and not completed. The test is built upon specific properties of the ED algorithm which enable to deduce for any instant, the maximum quantity of processor idle time that can be recovered to process the sporadic tasks. In section IV, we will recall the theoretical foundation for this approach and report an optimal acceptance algorithm under less restrictive assumptions.
To obtain any analytical results about program behavior in hard real-time environment, certain assumptions must be made about this environment. We shal define them precisely in this section.

div.head: 1-Scheduling periodic tasks
div.p: Let assume a monoprocessor machine which executes a periodic task set 2: during all the lifetime of the application. 2: is described as follows: %=(Tj(Cj,Pi),i=l to n). In this characterization, task T i initially makes a request for execution at time zero and therefore at times kPi (k=1,2, ...) with Pi being the period of Ti. The execution time required for each request of T i is Ci time units and a deadline occurs Pi time after each request by which T i must have completed its execution. Throughout our discussion, we assume that a preemptive scheduling discipline is employed. Thus, a request of Ci units of execution time can be satisfied by one or more quanta which sum to Ci. There is no inter-task communication during task execution and task don't use any critical resource.

The fundamental property of the schedule produced by any preemptive algorithm and in particular by ED on 2: is its cyclicity [Leung 801. Let P=LCM(Pi,P2, ..., P,) the base period be equal to the least common multiple of the periods P1,P2, ..., Pn. Let us assume 2: is feasibly scheduled by ED.

This property means that the processor does exactly the same thing at time t>O that it does at time t+kP (K=1,2, ... ). So, studying the form of the schedule produced over an infinite length by ED amounts to studying the form of the schedule on the intervals [kP,(k+l)P], each of them being called a window. So, the schedule produced by ED for an infinite time period can be considered as a time rigid one in the sense that all requests of any task are started at a predetermined absolute point in time. It comes that the timing position of the processor idle time intervals can be perfectly known over the time interval [O,P] and consequently over any window.

The most common way for implementing ED consists in ordering all ready tasks by increasing deadline (ties are broken arbitrarily) and executing them as soon as possible. ED is obviously an on-line algorithm since it only requires timing characteristics of tasks that are ready at any time. Such implementation of ED is called Earliest Deadline as Soon as possible (EDS). By opposition, we may imagine an implementation of ED that amounts to executing tasks as late as possible. Finally, a key issue in the design of a scheduling scheme is to determine an appropriate way to consider its overhead. Here, overhead induced by scheduling comes from the total time spent for selection of the next task to be run and context switching at any scheduling point e.g any release time or completion time and moreover from the total time spent for implementing the acceptance routine whenever a sporadic task occurs.

As described in [Ramadtham 841, the former may be easily evaluated and then included in every tasks execution time in order to be accounted for the schedulability analysis achieved at the initialization time and for the acceptance of the sporadic tasks.

It is clear that the latter is increased in proportion of the computational complexity of the acceptance routine. So, in hard real time context where all the tasks must imperatively meet their timing requirements, it is of more practical interest to make use of an algorithm which is not only optimal in term of scheduling performance but as efficient as possible in term of complexity.

The acceptance test proposed in this paper runs in O(N+m(z)) time in the worst case. Nevertheless, however little the overhead is, it must be taken into account, first by preventing that execution of the acceptance test will not cause accepted tasks to miss their deadlines and second by considering in the acceptance algorithm, the delay incurred by its execution. For this purpose, it suffices to incorporate with the sporadic task set, an additional task which execution time is equal to the execution time of the acceptance routine and which deadline is less than that of all the sporadic tasks. Unfortunately, we may gather from a preliminary study that, for the former problem, no resolution scheme which is both simple and fully satisfactory seems to exist.

div.head: v-CO-
div.p: In this paper, we have presented an approach for solving the problem of dynamically scheduling tasks in a hard real-time system, where all the tasks are independent and have strict deadlines. The crux of our aproach lies in a specific property of the Earliest Deadline algorithm stated in [Chetto 89al which enables us to use the entire processing power of the machine. Furthermore, considering precedence constraints among sporadic tasks can be achieved easily while preserving efficiency and optimality of our acceptance algorithm. A recent study reported in [Chetto 89b] shows how to transform a set of dependent tasks into a set of independent tasks. This transformation is proved to be optimal in the sense that a valid schedule can be obtained for the former one if and only if a valid schedule can be obtained for the latter one. It consists in a specific modification of timing parameters of tasks that insures that in any schedule produced by Earliest Deadline algorithm all the precedence constraints w i l l be obeyed implicitly. It follows that we may apply this transformation to denendent snoradic tasks and then use our optimal decision algorithm. So, the work described in this paper is an extension of our work but also contributes in the field of real-time preemptive scheduling.
